chapters.1: Paul addresses reports of division in the Corinthian church, where believers have split into factions following different leaders. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified, though it seems foolish by worldly standards, is actually God's wisdom and power, and that God chose ordinary, humble people rather than the worldly-wise to make this point clear.
chapters.2: Paul recalls that he deliberately avoided impressive rhetoric when he first preached to the Corinthians, relying instead on the Spirit's power so their faith would rest on God, not human cleverness. He explains that spiritual truths, hidden from the world's wisdom, are revealed by the Holy Spirit to those who have the Spirit of God.
chapters.3: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for their immaturity, shown by their jealousy and quarreling over which leader they prefer. He explains that he and other leaders are merely servants working together for God, and warns that each person's ministry will be tested, like building materials tried by fire, while God's people themselves are his holy temple.
chapters.4: Paul describes apostles as servants and stewards entrusted with God's mysteries, answerable ultimately to God rather than human judgment. He contrasts his own hardships and humility with the Corinthians' apparent self-satisfied pride, urging them to imitate his example and warning that he will soon visit to address their arrogance directly.
chapters.5: Paul confronts the church for tolerating a serious case of sexual immorality in their midst instead of dealing with it, comparing unaddressed sin to leaven that spreads through the whole batch of dough. He instructs them to remove the unrepentant member from their fellowship, clarifying that this kind of discipline applies to those inside the church, not to outsiders.
chapters.6: Paul criticizes believers for taking disputes with each other to secular courts rather than resolving them within the church. He also warns against sexual immorality, reminding the Corinthians that their bodies belong to God as temples of the Holy Spirit and were bought at the price of Christ's sacrifice.
chapters.7: Paul answers questions about marriage, singleness, and sexuality, affirming that both marriage and remaining single are valid callings depending on a person's circumstances and gifts. He advises believers to remain in their current marital and social situations where possible, focusing on undivided devotion to the Lord, especially given the urgency of the times.
chapters.8: Paul addresses whether believers may eat food previously offered to idols, acknowledging that idols have no real power but cautioning that exercising this freedom carelessly could harm a fellow believer whose conscience is weaker. He concludes that love for others should outweigh personal liberty when it risks causing someone else to stumble.
chapters.9: Paul defends his right as an apostle to receive support for his ministry, though he explains that he voluntarily gave up that right to avoid hindering the gospel. He describes adapting himself to different people in order to win them for Christ, and compares his disciplined Christian life to an athlete training for a race.
chapters.10: Paul warns the Corinthians using Israel's wilderness history as an example, showing that privileged spiritual experience did not protect the Israelites from judgment when they gave in to idolatry and immorality. He urges believers to avoid idol worship, explaining how sharing in the Lord's Supper creates a spiritual bond, and to act with consideration for others' consciences in everyday matters like eating.
chapters.11: Paul addresses church order, including head coverings in worship reflecting the created relationship between men and women, and then strongly rebukes the Corinthians for selfish and unequal behavior at their communal meals before the Lord's Supper. He reiterates the words Jesus used when instituting the Lord's Supper and urges self-examination before participating.
chapters.12: Paul describes the variety of spiritual gifts given by the Holy Spirit to different believers for the common good, emphasizing that no gift is more essentially important than another. He uses the image of the human body, with its many different but interdependent parts, to illustrate how the church functions together as one body in Christ.
chapters.13: Paul writes his famous description of love, explaining that spiritual gifts and impressive achievements mean nothing without genuine love, which is patient, kind, and selfless. He concludes that while spiritual gifts like prophecy and knowledge will eventually pass away, love is the greatest and most enduring virtue of all.
chapters.14: Paul compares the gifts of prophecy and speaking in tongues, favoring prophecy because it is immediately understandable and builds up the whole church, while tongues require interpretation to be useful in public worship. He calls for orderly, edifying worship services where everything is done decently and in proper order.
chapters.15: Paul defends the reality of Christ's resurrection as the foundation of the Christian faith, listing eyewitnesses who saw the risen Jesus, and argues that if Christ wasn't raised, Christian faith would be meaningless. He goes on to describe the future resurrection of believers, explaining that their bodies will be transformed from perishable to imperishable, concluding with a triumphant declaration that death has been defeated.
chapters.16: Paul gives practical instructions about collecting a financial offering for the believers in Jerusalem and shares his travel plans to visit Corinth after passing through Macedonia. He closes with personal greetings, encouragement to stand firm in the faith, and a final blessing.
